confirmed.title: A district-name search lands on a same-named village far away, and the real district is dropped as a duplicate
confirmed.description: An exact match never gets the distance penalty (`!exact && e.d > PENALTY_FROM_M`). Every exact town also gets +50 (line 327). So two OSM town nodes with the same name end up with exactly the same score, and `scored.sort` (line 332) leaves them in data-file order. The dedupe at line 342 then drops any later entry with the same folded name and the same kind (`o.kind === e.kind`), however far apart the two are. When the village comes first in the data, it becomes the top hit and the real district centre never appears. The same rule also puts a far village above the correct station or pier when the city has no real town node for that name.
confirmed.failure_scenario: In İzmir, search 'Menderes'. The top hit is a 'Menderes' town at 38.1034,28.20324, about 95 km from the district centre in cities.ts (38.2552,27.1381). The real Menderes town node (38.25516,27.13814) is removed as a duplicate. In Antalya, 'Kemer' gives the town at 36.35859,29.71369, about 80 km away; the real Kemer (36.60138,30.56386) is dropped. In İstanbul, 'Kadıköy' or 'kadikoy' gives a 'Kadıköy' village at 41.11009,29.90481 in Şile, about 75 km out. It is ranked above the actual Kadıköy pier and station. None of these hits gets `far`, because they are inside the province box. A user who taps the first suggestion is sent to the wrong place.
confirmed.evidence: search.ts:322-327 `const far = !exact && e.d > PENALTY_FROM_M ? ... : 0; ... if (exact && e.kind === 'town') adjust += 50;`; search.ts:332 `scored.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score);` (ties stay in data order); search.ts:339-344 dedupe `fold(o.name) === e.key && (o.kind === e.kind || e.d > FAR_M || ...)`. data/places-izmir.json has two 'Menderes' k:'town' rows, with (38.1034, 28.20324) listed before (38.25516, 27.13814). data/places-istanbul.json has only two 'Kadıköy' towns, at (41.11009,29.90481) and (41.13665,28.36367). Probe output: `istanbul Kadıköy [{name:'Kadıköy',kind:'town',lat:41.11009,lng:29.90481}, {name:'Kadiköy',kind:'pier',...,district:'Üsküdar'}, ...]` and `izmir Menderes [{name:'Menderes',kind:'town',lat:38.1034,lng:28.20324}, ...]`.

votes.reason:
The finding is real. I traced the code and ran it with bun, calling searchPlaces after setActiveCity.

Code behaviour (src/data/search.ts):
- Line 323: `far` is 0 whenever `exact` is true, so distance never lowers an exact match.
- Line 320: `near` only applies inside 6 km (NEAR_CITY_M), so both same-named towns get 0 there.
- Line 327: every exact town gets +50.
- Result: two exact 'town' rows with the same name get exactly the same score, and the stable sort at line 332 keeps them in data-file order.
- Lines 339-344: the dedupe drops any later entry with the same folded name and the same kind (`o.kind === e.kind`), whatever the distance between them. So the second town is thrown away.

Probe output:
- izmir 'Menderes' / 'menderes': top hit is town (38.1034, 28.20324). The real district centre (38.25516, 27.13814) is not in the list at all; the Menderes station and Belediyesi rows rank lower.
- antalya 'Kemer': top hit is town (36.35859, 29.71369). The real Kemer town is missing; hits further down (Kemer Devlet Hastanesi, etc.) are in the real Kemer.
- istanbul 'Kadıköy' / 'kadikoy': top hit is town (41.11009, 29.90481), which is in Şile. It ranks above the actual Kadıköy pier and station, which show at (40.99, 29.02).
- None of these hits has `far: true`.

Impact: searchPlaces(q, 1)[0] is also used for chat place resolution (search.ts:401, intent.ts:245/256). So a plain district name, including a major one like Kadıköy, sends the user or the assistant 75-95 km away. This is a real wrong result on common, everyday queries.

I could not refute this. I ran the live code with a read-only Jest probe kept in the scratchpad (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-yerim-var-/902fb8fc-47be-5524-ab3f-5d7563989f0e/scratchpad/probe/probe.test.ts), which calls setActiveCity and then searchPlaces. Every case in the finding came out as described.

Results:
- izmir 'Menderes' and 'menderes': the top hit is the town at 38.1034,28.20324. The real Menderes town at 38.25516,27.13814 is not in the results; only the station and two area entries come after it.
- antalya 'Kemer': the top hit is the town at 36.35859,29.71369. The real Kemer town at 36.60138,30.56386 is missing from the results.
- istanbul 'Kadıköy' and 'kadikoy': the top hit is the town at 41.11009,29.90481 (a village in Şile). It ranks above the real Kadıköy pier and station.

Why it happens:
- At search.ts:322-323, an exact match gets no `far` penalty.
- Both same-named towns are too far from the city centre to get the `near` bonus (NEAR_CITY_M is 6 km).
- Both get the same rank*5 score and the same +50 exact-town bonus, so their scores are identical.
- `scored.sort` is stable, so the tie stays in data-file order. In places-izmir.json the far Menderes row comes before the real one; the Kemer rows in places-antalya.json are in the same order.
- The dedupe at line 342 (`o.kind === e.kind`) then drops the second town with the same name, however far apart the two are.
- None of the wrong hits gets `far: true`, because they are inside the province area.

Reachability:
- The bug is in normal use, with no special input needed. Typing a district name into place search reaches it.
- The chat assistant also reaches it. searchPlacesStrict hands queries over 6 letters straight to searchPlaces (search.ts:366), and assistant.ts:754 and :1317 take `searchPlacesStrict(it.placeQuery, 1)[0]`. So a chat request naming Menderes, Kemer or Kadıköy silently resolves to a place 75-95 km away.

Severity is high: these are district names in three of the five cities, the result is a wrong destination with no warning, and the correct district centre is removed from the list.

The bug is real. I ran a scratchpad jest probe against the actual searchPlaces and got the results the finding describes. İzmir 'Menderes' and 'menderes' both put the town at 38.1034,28.20324 first, and the real Menderes town (38.25516,27.13814) is gone from the list. Antalya 'Kemer' puts the town at 36.35859,29.71369 first and drops the real Kemer (36.60138,30.56386). İstanbul 'Kadıköy' and 'kadikoy' put the Şile village at 41.11009,29.90481 above the Kadıköy pier and station. None of these hits is marked `far`.

The cause is in src/data/search.ts. Line 322-323 skips the distance penalty for exact matches, and line 327 gives every exact town +50. The `near` bonus only applies within 6 km of the city centre, so both same-named towns usually get exactly the same score. The sort at line 332 then keeps data-file order. The dedupe at lines 339-344 (`o.kind === e.kind || e.d > FAR_M`) drops the second town however far away it is. In data/places-izmir.json the far Menderes row comes before the real one, and data/places-antalya.json has the same order for Kemer.

This is not intended behaviour. The comment "An exact name is what the user typed: distance never demotes it" (commit 6f4e2ac) is about ranking an exact name above prefix matches. Nothing says the data-file order should pick between two exact towns, and no test covers this case.

User impact: searchPlaces feeds the suggestion lists in src/lib/usePlaceSearch.ts, which src/app/yer-ara.tsx and TypingState use. Town hits show no district label, so the wrong first suggestion looks the same as the real one, and tapping it centres the user 75-95 km away.

Why medium and not high: the district flow in the chat goes through the district list in cities.ts (intent.test expects 'Menderes' to resolve as a district). The nearby station, pier or hospital entries also still appear lower in the same list. So users are not fully blocked, but the top suggestion is wrong in several real districts.

confirmed.title: Per-IP guard uses the full client IP, so rotating IPv6 addresses (plus free deviceIds) removes every per-client limit and lets one attacker use up the global daily cap for all users
confirmed.description: The client picks deviceId freely (any /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/), so the per-device limits (FREE_DAILY=10, the 1 s interval, MAX_CANCELS_PER_DAY) do nothing against an abuser. The comment on ipGuard says the per-IP counter is the defence against deviceId rotation. That counter is keyed on the raw CF-Connecting-IP string (`ip:${day}:${ip}`). For IPv6 clients this is the full /128 address, and any ordinary IPv6 host or VPS controls at least a /64 (2^64 addresses). An attacker who changes both the source address and the deviceId on each request never meets the per-IP or per-device limit. Only AI_GLOBAL_DAILY (10000) stops them. Once that cap is reached, every real user in all five cities gets 429 reason "global" (the app shows its 'busy' fallback) for the rest of the Istanbul day. The attacker also spends the whole daily Anthropic budget: 10000 new messages, each followed by unmetered same-fingerprint /pick or /plan retries, each up to 1024-2048 output tokens. A side effect pointing the other way: one IPv4 address shared by many users behind carrier-grade NAT (common on Turkish mobile networks) shares a single 100-call budget. Every stage of one message (/understand plus /pick or /plan or /narrate) and every rejected 'slow' attempt counts toward it, so honest users behind a busy CGNAT address get 429 reason 'ip' after about 33 messages in total.
confirmed.failure_scenario: An attacker on an IPv6 /64 loops POST /understand. Each request uses a fresh source address, a fresh random deviceId and a fresh messageId. ipGuard(ip) sees count 0 every time and lets it through. takeUse sees a new device with no 'last' key and charges it. After about 10000 requests, ai:global:<day> >= limits.global, and every legitimate POST /understand returns 429 {error:'rate_limited', reason:'global'} until Istanbul midnight. The attacker has paid nothing, and the operator has paid for 10000+ Anthropic calls.
confirmed.evidence: index.ts:194-196: `const ip = req.headers.get('CF-Connecting-IP') ?? 'unknown'; ... if (!(await quota.ipGuard(ip, now, limits.perIp)))`. quota.ts:102-104: `/** Per-IP daily call counter; false when over max (stops device-id rotation abuse). */ export async function ipGuard(kv, ip, now, max = 100) { const key = `ip:${todayIstanbul(now)}:${ip}`;`. quota.ts:272: `const ID_RE = /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/;` is the only deviceId check (no attestation). quota.ts:192: the global cap is the only limit that does not depend on a client-chosen key.

votes.reason:
I traced the code and it behaves as the finding says.

- **Per-IP key is the raw address.** index.ts:194-196 reads `CF-Connecting-IP` and calls `quota.ipGuard(ip, now, limits.perIp)`. quota.ts:103-104 builds the key as `ip:${todayIstanbul(now)}:${ip}`. Nothing normalises IPv6 to a /64 prefix, so each IPv6 address gets its own counter. That counter is the defence the comment says "stops device-id rotation abuse".
- **deviceId is free and unverified.** The only check on it is `ID_RE = /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/` (quota.ts:272). No attestation exists anywhere.
- **New devices pass the other limits.** For a new deviceId, the `ai:last:${deviceId}` key does not exist, so the 'slow' check passes. The per-device list is empty, so `charge` succeeds. After that, the only thing standing in the way is `ai:global:${day}` checked against `limits.global` (quota.ts:192).
- **The global cap becomes a shutdown lever.** wrangler.toml sets AI_GLOBAL_DAILY="10000" and AI_DAILY_PER_IP="100", and there is no Cloudflare rate-limit binding or other limiter.
- **Failure scenario.** An attacker on one IPv6 /64 sends requests, each with a fresh source address, deviceId and messageId. After about 10000 requests the global counter is full. Every real user then gets 429 reason 'global' until Istanbul midnight. The operator also pays for those Anthropic calls.

**Why medium, not high.**
- The Anthropic spend is still limited by the global cap, which is there by design, so the money at risk is the budget the operator already chose.
- The real impact is a denial of service for all users, triggered without credentials.
- The same attack also works without IPv6: about 100 IPv4 proxies would be enough. IPv6 just makes it free.
- The CGNAT point (shared IPv4 users reaching the 100-call limit) is real but less important.

I could not refute this from the code. Every part of the path can be reached.

1. The endpoints are public and need no login. index.ts:163-189 accepts POST /understand from anyone who sends a valid body, and the only device check is ID_RE (quota.ts:272), so a client can make up any deviceId it wants.
2. The per-IP limit is keyed on the raw CF-Connecting-IP string. At index.ts:194-196, ipGuard(ip, now, limits.perIp) builds the key `ip:${todayIstanbul(now)}:${ip}` (quota.ts:102-104). Nothing groups IPv6 addresses into a /64 prefix. Cloudflare serves Workers over IPv6 by default, so one host with a /64 can send each request from a new address and the counter starts at 0 every time.
3. takeUse (quota.ts:182-200) only checks the 1 s interval against ai:last:<deviceId>, so a new deviceId skips it. A new deviceId also starts with an empty daily list, so it gets charged and the global counter goes up by one.
4. The repo has nothing else in front of this: wrangler.toml has no rate-limit binding, and no Turnstile or app attestation exists anywhere. The only limit that does not depend on a client-chosen key is AI_GLOBAL_DAILY = 10000. worker.test.ts:249 confirms that every request returns 429 reason 'global' once that cap is reached.

So one attacker can use up the shared daily cap, and every real user then gets the fallback until Istanbul midnight. An attacker does not even need IPv6: about 100 IPv4 proxies at 100 calls each also reach 10000.

Severity: medium, not high. The global cap does what it was built to do, which is limit Anthropic spend to about 10000 messages a day. The real impact is a daily denial of service for all users and running up cost to that cap. There is no data leak and no unlimited spend. The CGNAT side effect is also real: perIp=100 counts every stage and every rejected 'slow' attempt. But that one is about choosing the limit, not an exploitable hole.

I confirmed this from the code. The deviceId is whatever the client sends: the only check is ID_RE (quota.ts:272), so the per-device limits do not stop a client that rotates IDs. The comment on ipGuard (quota.ts:102) says the per-IP counter is the defence against device-id rotation. That counter is keyed on the raw CF-Connecting-IP string (`ip:${todayIstanbul(now)}:${ip}`, quota.ts:104; called at index.ts:194-196), with no grouping of IPv6 addresses into a /64 or any other prefix. I found nothing that adds another layer: no Turnstile, no attestation, no Cloudflare rate-limit rule in wrangler.toml, and no mention of IPv6 anywhere in the repo. So a client rotating IPv6 addresses inside its own /64 never reaches perIp. The only limit left is AI_GLOBAL_DAILY (10000). Once that is used up, takeUse returns reason 'global' for every new message from every real user until Istanbul midnight (quota.ts:192). So the bypass the comment says is closed is in fact open. It lets one client deny AI service to every user for the rest of the day.

Two things lower the severity. First, the global cap does exactly what it was designed to do: it holds Anthropic spending to the budget the operator set, so the cost side ("pays for 10000+ calls") is the intended worst case, not runaway spending. Second, even without IPv6 the same attack needs only about 100 IPv4 addresses, which are easy to get through proxies, so IPv6 makes it cheaper rather than creating a new class of attack. What remains is a whole-day denial of AI service for all users that one client can trigger, plus a per-IP guard that does not do what its comment says. I rate it medium, not high.

confirmed.title: settleDistrict's fuzzy text scan turns everyday words into far-off districts (çabuk->Çubuk, serin->Serik, tuzlu->Tuzla, evden->Evren)
confirmed.description: When the AI returns a search with no district (and nearMe false), settled() runs districtInText over every word of the user's message. matchDistrict accepts any word of 5+ letters that is within one Damerau edit (two from 8 letters) of a district and shares its first letter. Many common chat words pass that test against a real district of the active city. The made-up district then becomes next.place at assistant.ts:1304, so the search moves to that district's centre. The rule parser does not do this: it only allows typos on leftover place tokens, and only in İzmir. The test list of words that must not match (kebap, lahmacun, yemek, ...) has no word that lands one edit away from a district.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Ankara, AI router on: the user types "çabuk bir şeyler yiyelim". The AI gives search {food:true, district:null, place:null, nearMe:false, wishes:[quick]}. districtInText reads 'çabuk' (folded 'cabuk'), which is one edit from 'cubuk', so the district becomes Çubuk and the user gets restaurants about 40 km north instead of near them. The same happens in Antalya with "serin bir mekan" (Serik) and "kepek ekmeği" (Kepez), in Istanbul with "tuzlu bir şeyler" (Tuzla), in Ankara with "evden çıktım, ..." (Evren), and in İzmir with "kiraz" (Kiraz) or "konuk" (Konak).
confirmed.evidence: districtMatch.ts:73-76: `if (s.length < 5 || s[0] !== n[0]) continue; const cost = edits(s, n); if (cost <= (n.length >= 8 ? 2 : 1) ...) best = { name, cost };` and :128-130 `const found = districtInText(text, districts, skip); return found ? { ...s, district: found } : s;`. I re-implemented the same fold, stems and edits logic in node and got: çabuk->Çubuk, serin->Serik, evden->Evren, tuzlu->Tuzla, kepek->Kepez, konuk->Konak, sisli->Şişli, kiraz->Kiraz. assistant.ts:1084 applies settleDistrict to every AI search.

votes.reason: The finding is real; I traced it in the code and reproduced it. In src/data/districtMatch.ts, settled() (lines 117-131) handles an AI search that has no district, no district-like place and nearMe false: it calls districtInText(text, districts, skip) on the raw user text. The skip list only holds dish, place and dishServes. districtInText passes every word to matchDistrict. For any district name of 5 or more letters, matchDistrict accepts a stem of 5 or more letters with the same first letter and a Damerau distance of 1 or less (2 or less for names of 8+ letters) (lines 72-76). Nothing checks whether the word is an ordinary Turkish word. The districts are real entries in src/data/cities.ts: Kiraz:74, Konak:75, Tuzla:124, Çubuk:139, Evren:142, Kepez:194, Serik:200. I copied districtMatch.ts and fold() unchanged into the scratchpad and ran them with node. settleDistrict({kind:'search',district:null,place:null,nearMe:false,food:true}, text, districts) returned these districts: "çabuk bir şeyler yiyelim" -> Çubuk, "evden çıktım aç kaldım" -> Evren, "serin bir mekan" -> Serik, "kepek ekmeği" -> Kepez, "tuzlu bir şeyler" -> Tuzla, "konuk geldi" -> Konak. Downstream, assistant.ts:1084 applies settleDistrict to every AI-routed search. intentFromUnderstanding (assistant.ts:439) turns u.district into a districtCenter. aiLedIntent (assistant.ts:481-494) keeps ai.district and does not override it with the rule parse. At assistant.ts:~1304, `if (it.district) next.place = {label: it.district.name, lat, lng}` moves the search to that district's centre, for example Çubuk, about 40 km from central Ankara. Limits: this needs the AI router on and an AI reply with district=null and nearMe=false. The AI may set nearMe for some of these phrases, and that would skip the scan. The result is wrong recommendations, not a crash or a data leak, so I rate it medium rather than high.

I could not refute this. The bug is real and real users can reach it in production, though the finding's own examples are weaker than a case it missed.

How it is reached: app.json sets extra.aiUrl (https://yerim-ai.patrickgt966.workers.dev), so the AI router is on in shipped builds. For every AI search that is not a follow-up, assistant.ts:1084 calls settleDistrict(routed.out.value, text, activeCity().districts). When the AI gives no district and nearMe is false, settled() (districtMatch.ts:126-130) scans every word of the message with districtInText. matchDistrict:74-76 accepts any stem of 5+ letters that has the same first letter and is within 1 edit (2 edits for names of 8+ letters) of a district.

What I ran: the real module under jest, using a test file in the scratchpad (no repo files touched). Results: 'çabuk bir şeyler yiyelim' gives Çubuk (Ankara), 'serin bir mekan' gives Serik and 'kepek ekmeği' gives Kepez (Antalya), 'tuzlu bir şeyler' gives Tuzla (İstanbul), 'evden çıktım' gives Evren (Ankara), 'konuk' gives Konak (İzmir).

Where I would push back: the router prompt (protocol.ts:400) tells the AI to set nearMe=true for food requests that name no place ('acıktım'). That makes settled() return early at :126, so the bare examples like 'çabuk bir şeyler yiyelim' may often be safe. In 'kepek ekmeği' the AI would probably set dish to that phrase, and then the skip list removes the word.

A worse case the finding missed: the user names a place that is not a district, so the AI correctly sets nearMe=false and place=X. I ran settleDistrict on these:
- {place:'Kızılay', wishes:[quick]} with "Kızılay'da çabuk bir şeyler yiyelim" (Ankara) gives district Çubuk.
- "evden çıktım kızılayda kebap" gives Evren.
- "kadıköy çarşıda tuzlu bir şeyler" (İstanbul) gives Tuzla.
- "konuk gelecek alsancakta meyhane" (İzmir) gives Konak.

The invented district then wins. intentFromUnderstanding (assistant.ts:439-441) turns it into a district centre. At assistant.ts:1303-1307, `if (it.district) next.place = ... {label: it.district.name, lat, lng}` runs before `else if (it.placeQuery)`. districtLeftover returns null when a cat is set (assistant.ts:340). So the place the user named is dropped and the search moves to a district tens of km away, such as Çubuk instead of Kızılay.

Why medium and not high: this gives users plainly wrong results on a core flow, triggered by common Turkish words. There is no crash, security issue or data loss, and the bare-message variants are partly covered by the nearMe=true prompt rule.

I could not refute this. I ran the real module with bun on the real city lists from cities.ts. districtInText returned these: Ankara 'çabuk bir şeyler yiyelim' -> Çubuk, 'evden çıktım' -> Evren; Istanbul 'tuzlu bir şeyler' -> Tuzla, 'sisli bir hava' -> Şişli; Antalya 'serin bir mekan' -> Serik, 'kepek ekmeği' -> Kepez; İzmir 'konuk geldi' -> Konak.

The cause is matchDistrict at districtMatch.ts:74-76. It allows one edit for any stem of 5+ letters that shares the district's first letter, and it has no list of common words to ignore. settled() at :126-130 runs this over every word of the user's text whenever the AI gives no district and nearMe is false. assistant.ts:1084 applies it to every AI search. That district then becomes next.place (assistant.ts:1303-1307), so the search moves to that district's centre.

None of this is intended. The docstring and the 'is not fooled by other words' test show the goal is to avoid false hits. The test words (kebap, yemek, ...) are not one edit from any district, so the test cannot catch the problem. This code came in with a single commit (54f5cea) and has no exceptions for common words.

Some things limit the impact:
- The prompt (protocol.ts:400) asks for nearMe=true on food requests that name no place, such as 'acıktım'. Then this path is skipped. Line 415, however, says nearMe is true only for explicit near-me phrases. So for phrases like 'serin bir mekan', 'tuzlu bir şeyler' or 'konuk geldi ne yesek', nearMe=false is likely.
- When the AI marks a phrase as the dish ('kepek ekmeği'), those words are skipped.
- 'kiraz' -> Kiraz is a real exact district name, so it does not count as a typo match.

What the user sees is a search placed in a wrong district, sometimes 40 km away (Çubuk). The app does not crash and no data leaks. I would rate this medium, not high.

confirmed.title: A district scraped from elsewhere in the text overrides the place the AI named
confirmed.description: settled() only leaves out the words of the AI's place when it scans for a district. When the AI put a non-district place in place (a quarter such as Alsancak or Karaköy, where the prompt tells it to leave district empty), any other district word in the sentence is still added as district. Examples are a starting point, a district the user ruled out, or a comparison. In answerText the district always beats the place: districtLeftover returns null as soon as a cat is set, and next.place becomes the district centre. The place the AI read correctly is thrown away.
confirmed.failure_scenario: İzmir: "Karşıyaka'dan geçiyorum, Alsancak'ta balık". The AI gives {place:'Alsancak', district:null, cat:'fish'}. districtInText skips 'alsancak' but matches "karşıyaka'dan", so district becomes Karşıyaka. Because it.cat is set, districtLeftover returns null and next.place is Karşıyaka's centre: fish places in Karşıyaka, not Alsancak. The same goes for "Bornova'da değil, Alsancak'ta kahve" and "Kadıköy'den Karaköy'e geçeceğim, kokoreç" (Istanbul). Without a cat, the user gets the districtUnknownThing reply ("Karşıyaka'da 'alsancak' ...") or Alsancak is dropped by the DISTRICT_REACH_M filter.
confirmed.evidence: districtMatch.ts:126-130: `if (s.nearMe) return s; const skip = [s.dish, s.place, ...]; const found = districtInText(text, districts, skip); return found ? { ...s, district: found } : s;` (it does not stop when s.place is set). assistant.ts:340 `if (it.cat || it.mentionsParking || it.nearMe || ...) return null;` and assistant.ts:1304-1308 `if (it.district) { next.place = left?.kind === 'place' ? left.place : { label: it.district.name, ... } } else if (it.placeQuery) {...}`.

votes.reason:
I traced the code and the finding holds. In src/data/districtMatch.ts settled() at lines 116-131, when the AI returns {district:null, place:'Alsancak'}, matchDistrict('Alsancak') finds nothing, because Alsancak is not in İzmir's district list in cities.ts. nearMe is false, so the code reaches `districtInText(text, districts, skip)`, where skip holds only dish, place and dishServes. The words are split on /[^\p{L}'’]+/, so "karşıyaka'dan" stays one token. key() folds it to "karsiyakadan", stems() removes "dan", and the result matches "karsiyaka" exactly. So district becomes Karşıyaka and place stays 'Alsancak'.

In assistant.ts:1084, settleDistrict feeds intentFromUnderstanding (lines 435-458), which gives district = Karşıyaka's centre and placeQuery = 'alsancak'. In districtLeftover (lines 338-340), `if (it.cat || ...) return null` fires because cat is 'fish', so left is null. At lines 1304-1308, `if (it.district)` sets next.place to Karşıyaka's centre. The placeQuery branch is an else-if, so it never runs and the place the AI read is dropped.

Nothing in settled() stops the text scan when s.place is already set. The function's own doc comment says a district is taken from the text only when there is no district, and it never considers that the AI may have deliberately filled place with a quarter. Wrong-location results follow for sentences that mention a district word as a starting point, an exclusion or a comparison next to a quarter name. confirmed.title: Opening-hours parser treats most bundled restaurant hours ("Mo-Su HH:MM-HH:MM", "24/7") as unknown
confirmed.description: The restaurant hours come straight from OSM `opening_hours` (data/food-*.json key `h`) and are passed to openState/closesLate as `openingHoursText` (src/data/assistant.ts:1590, 1594, 1705, 1729, 2514). fromText only accepts a bare `HH:MM–HH:MM` first segment (RANGE at line 20, `if (!range) return 'unknown'` at line 41), and closesLate does the same check (line ~102). confirmed.title: scorePick passes any 'nothing fits' answer when the case did not set noneFit
confirmed.description: scorePick only checks noneFit when the case sets `e.noneFit`, and it skips all pickIn/notFit checks whenever the model says `p.noneFit === true`. Almost every pick case leaves noneFit unset: 5 of the 6 PICK_CASES, the 36 non-noneFit BIG_PICK_CASES, and all 42 EXTREME_PICK_CASES (buildHardPicks only sets `{ pickIn: good }`). So if the model gives up and answers noneFit:true, the case still passes, even when suitable candidates were offered. toPick (protocol.ts:702-704) accepts noneFit:true with any or no pick index, so nothing upstream catches it either. aiScore.test.ts only tests noneFit on the case that expects it.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Case 'vegetarian: a lokanta fits, a butcher does not' (expect { pickIn:[2], notFit:[0,3,4] }). The model answers { noneFit:true, pick:0, fit:[] }. Line 92 is skipped because e.noneFit is undefined, line 96 is skipped because p.noneFit is true, misses stay [] and the result is pass:true. In the app the user is told nothing fits even though the lokanta does, and the live eval (BIG_PASS 80% gate) still reports PASS. A model that always says 'none fits' would pass every pick_hard case.

The finding is real. I traced it line by line and it holds.

**How scorePick behaves (src/data/eval/aiScore.ts:88-104)**
- Line 92 checks noneFit only when the case sets `e.noneFit` (`e.noneFit !== undefined && p.noneFit !== e.noneFit`).
- Line 96 (`if (!p.noneFit) {...}`) skips the pickIn and notFit checks whenever the model answers noneFit:true.

**Most cases never set noneFit**
- In aiCases.ts, 5 of the 6 PICK_CASES expect only `{ pickIn, notFit }`, for example `{ pickIn: [2], notFit: [0, 3, 4] }`. Only one expects `{ noneFit: true }`.
- aiBigCases.ts:1032-1034 produces `s.noneFit ? { noneFit: true } : { pickIn: at(s.good), notFit: at(s.bad) }`, so the non-noneFit cases never carry `noneFit: false`.
- aiExtremeCases.ts:866 and :991 produce `expect: { pickIn: good }`.

**Nothing upstream catches it**
- toPick (src/lib/ai/protocol.ts:702-704) sets `noneFit = raw.noneFit === true`.
- A missing pick then falls back to 0 (`?? (noneFit ? 0 : null)`), so an answer of `{noneFit:true}` comes through as a valid PickResponse.

**What that means for scores**
- A model answering `{noneFit:true, pick:0, fit:[]}` on the vegetarian case gets `misses=[]` and `pass:true`.
- scripts/ai-eval.ts:226 and scripts/ai-eval-big.ts:206 both score through this function. A model that always says "nothing fits" therefore passes every pick case except the noneFit-true ones.
- aiScore.test.ts:71-80 only tests noneFit:true against the case that expects it, so the tests do not cover this gap.

**Severity: medium, not high**
- This is a hole in the eval oracle. It is not a runtime bug in the app.
- Users only see the wrong "nothing fits" answer if the model actually regresses this way, and the eval would then fail to catch that regression.

confirmed.title: AI /pick requests leak the user's location (by triangulation) despite 'Konumun gönderilmez'
confirmed.description: For a 'near me' restaurant pick, the app sends up to 40 candidates (MAX_PICK_CANDIDATES=40). Each one carries the restaurant's real public name (withLabel, line 2326) and walkMin = walkMinFromMeters(card.distanceM), where distanceM is measured from the search target, which is the user's GPS fix when they search near themselves. The restaurant positions are public (OSM/Overture), so 40 (name, walking-minutes) pairs let the worker operator or Anthropic recover the user's position to roughly one walk-minute (about 60 m). The consent card (tr.ts:650-651: 'Konumun gönderilmez'), the profile privacy text (tr.ts:328-329) and docs/gizlilik.html ('Konumun (koordinatların) ... gönderilmez') all tell the user their location is not sent. Under KVKK the location is still personal data, because it can be derived from what is sent.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A user at home in Bornova accepts Yerim ✨ and asks 'yakınımda vejetaryen ne var, sen seç'. The /pick body contains e.g. {name:'X Kafe', walkMin:3}, {name:'Y Lokanta', walkMin:7} ... for 40 named places. Look up those names in the bundled data/food-izmir.json and intersect the walk-time circles, and you get the user's home location to about 100 m. That location then goes to Anthropic, while the consent text the user agreed to says it does not.
confirmed.evidence: src/data/assistant.ts:2284-2290 `walkMin: walkMinFromMeters(card.distanceM)`; :2326 `name: clipText(r.name, MAX_LABEL_CHARS)`; :2419 `rest.map((c, k) => withLabel(pickCandidate(c, k), c, deps.t))`; src/lib/ai/verify.ts:26-27 `Math.max(1, Math.round((m * 1.3) / 80))`; src/lib/ai/protocol.ts:27 `MAX_PICK_CANDIDATES = 40`; server/yerim-ai/src/index.ts:368-377 sends `JSON.stringify({ text, candidates })` to Anthropic; src/i18n/tr.ts:651 'Konumun gönderilmez.'

The worker's validPick (server/yerim-ai/src/quota.ts:530-540) keeps both walkMin and name, plus the city. index.ts:382 then sends JSON.stringify({ text, candidates }) to Anthropic. Up to 40 named public places, each with a walking time measured from the user, let anyone with the public OSM/Overture coordinates intersect the distance rings and recover the user's position to within tens of metres. This contradicts what the user is told: the consent text (tr.ts:651 'Konumun gönderilmez.'), the profile privacy text ('konumun gönderilmez') and docs/gizlilik.html:49 ('Konumun (koordinatların) ... gönderilmez'). The comment at index.ts:364, 'Candidates carry facts only (no names)', is also out of date, because names are now sent. Raw coordinates are never sent, so this is a derivable leak rather than a direct one. It is still a real mismatch between the privacy promise and the code under KVKK, so I rate it medium.

The attack itself is theoretical. Someone at the operator or at Anthropic would have to deliberately triangulate the user from rounded walk minutes (Math.round(m*1.3/80), coarse steps). The worker already sees the client's IP address, which is a rough location anyway. Users often type their district themselves ("Bornova"). The app also accepts sending ~100 m location to Apple Maps. There is no crash, no wrong result and no undisclosed data flow, only a possible wording tweak to the one-line consent card. That is a disclosure nit, not a privacy hole.

confirmed.title: Privacy manifest declares no collected data, but chat text and a persistent device ID go to the app's server and Anthropic
confirmed.description: ios.privacyManifests sets NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes to []. With AI consent, the app sends the user's typed messages and chat history, plus a random device ID that is stored on the phone, to the Cloudflare Worker, which forwards the text to Anthropic. The privacy policy says the server keeps quota counters tied to the device ID and IP for up to two days. Under Apple's definition this is collected data: User Content (other user content) and Identifiers (Device ID), for App Functionality. The empty manifest, and any App Store privacy label built from it, under-declares this.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The user enables Yerim AI and chats. Each request carries `deviceId` and the message text (src/lib/ai/client.ts:198 and 327 post `{ deviceId, ... }` to the server). The device ID is kept for up to two days on the server, and Anthropic receives the text. The shipped PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy still says nothing is collected. That breaks Apple's privacy-manifest and nutrition-label rules (Guideline 5.1.1/5.1.2) and can lead to an App Review rejection or a later compliance notice.
confirmed.evidence: app.json: `"NSPrivacyTracking": false, "NSPrivacyTrackingDomains": [], "NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes": []`; src/store/ai.ts:78-79 persists `deviceId`; src/lib/ai/client.ts:327 `post('/quota', { deviceId }, ...)`; docs/gizlilik.html: 'For the daily limit, counters tied to the device ID and IP address are kept for at most two days' and 'each chat message goes through our server (Cloudflare) to Anthropic's Claude model'.

- **Device ID.** src/store/ai.ts:37 creates a random deviceId and lines 78-79 save it on the phone. It is sent with every AI call (src/app/sohbet.tsx:139-166), with /quota (client.ts:327) and with /cancel (client.ts:198).
- **Server storage.** On the Worker, server/yerim-ai/src/quota.ts writes KV keys `q:${day}:${deviceId}` (line 61), `ai:last:${deviceId}` and `ip:${day}:${ip}` (line 103). Their expirationTtl is TTL_SECONDS = 172800 (line 42), which is 48 hours.
- **Third party.** The message text and chat history are forwarded to Anthropic. docs/gizlilik.html says so itself (lines 42/88), and lines 49/95 say the device-ID and IP counters are kept for up to two days.

Apple's rule exempts only data that is processed in real time and not kept. A persistent identifier stored for 48 hours does not qualify, and neither does user content sent to a third-party AI provider. So at least Identifiers > Device ID and User Content > Other User Content, both for App Functionality, should be declared. The empty array under-declares them. This is a real compliance and data-correctness problem in the shipped config. It is not a crash and does not give users wrong results.

Two points keep the severity at medium rather than high. App Store Connect privacy labels are filled in by hand, not built from this manifest. App Review does not reliably reject builds over this. The realistic risk is an inaccurate privacy report and a possible review or compliance problem.

(3) The server keeps it after the request is served. server/yerim-ai/src/index.ts:205 builds KV keys of the form `ai:call:<day>:<deviceId>:<messageId>`. quota.ts:42 sets `TTL_SECONDS = 172800` (2 days) and passes it as `expirationTtl` at quota.ts:68, 87 and 108. The IP is also stored, in `ip:<day>:<ip>` (quota.ts:104) from `CF-Connecting-IP` (index.ts:132/152/194).
(4) The message text and history go to Anthropic, a third party. docs/gizlilik.html:42 and 88 say so.

Apple counts data as "collected" when it leaves the device and you or a partner can access it for longer than it takes to serve the request in real time. A device ID kept for 48 hours in KV meets that test (Identifiers, Device ID, App Functionality). So does chat text sent to a third-party AI provider (User Content, Other User Content). The optional-disclosure exemption needs the collection to be infrequent and outside the app's main function. A chat feature used repeatedly does not fit, and consent alone does not exempt it.

The repo has no other declaration, such as a separate privacy-label config. The shipped PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy will therefore under-declare. This is a real compliance and App Review risk, not a runtime crash, so medium fits.

Confirmed from the code. app.json:23 declares `"NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes": []`, but data that Apple counts as "collected" leaves the device. Apple treats data as collected when it is kept longer than needed to serve the request in real time.

1. **Device ID.** It is generated and persisted on the phone (src/store/ai.ts:37, 78-79) and sent with every /chat, /quota and /cancel call (src/app/sohbet.tsx:139-166, src/lib/ai/refresh.ts:29). The server keys per-device counters on it (server/yerim-ai/src/index.ts:205 `ai:call:${day}:${deviceId}:...`) and stores them with `expirationTtl` 172800 s, i.e. 2 days (server/yerim-ai/src/store.ts:21-22, 59, 197). That is Identifiers > Device ID, used for App Functionality.
2. **Chat text and history.** These go through the Worker to Anthropic, a third party that keeps API inputs under its own retention policy. That is User Content > Other User Content, used for App Functionality.

The optional-disclosure exemption does not apply, because the data is sent on every AI message rather than infrequently. The repo's own privacy policy (docs/gizlilik.html lines 42-49 and 88-95) discloses both items, so the app's privacy disclosures contradict each other. Commit bf13fd2 ("App Store app.json") added the empty array, and no comment, test or doc explains it as deliberate. It most likely dates from before the AI server existed: ROADMAP says "Hesap ve kişisel veri gelince gizlilik metni ve App Store bilgileri değişir" ("when accounts and personal data arrive, the privacy text and App Store details change").

I rate it medium, not higher. Nothing crashes and no data leaks, and the user-facing policy is honest. The real harm is a false privacy manifest, and any App Store label built from it, on the release branch. That risks App Review rejection under 5.1.1/5.1.2 and misinforms users who rely on the label.

confirmed.title: Restaurant favorites from other cities disappear, and the list goes stale after a city switch
confirmed.description: favoriteRestaurants is one global list of ids. getRestaurant only looks in the active city's data, so a favorite saved in another city resolves to null and is filtered out with no message. The useMemo also depends only on [ids], not on the city. If the tab stays mounted while the city changes, it keeps showing the old city's restaurants, and parkingInfo then computes their parking against the new city's car parks, which finds none.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The user favorites two İstanbul restaurants, then switches the city to İzmir. The Favoriler tab shows 'favorites.emptyRestaurants', or only the İzmir ones; the İstanbul favorites look deleted until the user switches back. If the tab was already mounted, it instead shows the İstanbul restaurants with 'no car park nearby', because their parking is checked against İzmir car parks.

2. **The list goes stale after a city switch.** The `useMemo` depends only on `[ids]`. `RestaurantFavorites` is not keyed by city. confirmed.title: Restaurant-name prefix shortcut turns common dish searches into a list of far-away look-alike names
confirmed.description: Any text of two or more words that is the start of some restaurant's name skips the whole search. Category, dish ranking, district, AI reading, parking and radius are all ignored, and the reply lists only the restaurants whose names start with the text, sorted by distance with no limit on how far. Many dish phrases are also the start of a business name ("adana kebap", "çiğ köfte", "esnaf lokantası", "kuru fasulye" in İstanbul, "et lokantası"). The shortcut runs even after the AI read the message as a category search.
confirmed.failure_scenario: İzmir, user near Konak (38.437, 27.143) types "adana kebap". Reply: chat.foundName {name:'Adana Kebap Tire', count:1} with a single card 63,396 m away in Tire. confirmed.title: When the AI returns both a district and a place, the place is thrown away and the district centre is searched
confirmed.description: The understand prompt tells the model to put a quarter or venue in `place` and to also fill `district` when it knows which district that is ("district'i ancak hangi ilçede olduğunu biliyorsan doldur"). confirmed.failure_scenario: "Alsancak'ta balık" with AI {district:'Konak', place:'Alsancak', cat:'fish'} gives ctx.place {label:'Konak', 38.4189, 27.1287} and 'Konak civarında 26 balık', about 2.6 km from Alsancak (38.4392, 27.1438). confirmed.title: Rules search the district the user explicitly ruled out ("Bornova değil Buca'da")
confirmed.description: Negation is handled only for a food category right before the negating word. For a place, the words 'değil' / 'olmasın' are simply removed as NEGATION filler, and the first district token in the text becomes the district. That is the one the user rejected. If the first token is a non-district place, districtLeftover turns it into the search place. This path runs whenever the AI is unavailable (quota used up, timeout, error, AI off).
confirmed.failure_scenario: With the AI off: "Bornova değil Buca'da kebap" gives district Bornova and 'Bornova civarında … kebap'. "Konak olmasın Karşıyaka'da balık" searches Konak. confirmed.evidence:
rest = rest.filter((t) => !isParking(t) && !NEGATION.has(t));   // 'degil','olmasin' dropped
...
const districtAt = isOnePlaceName(tokens) ? -1 : tokens.findIndex(isDistrictName);  // first district wins
The notCat loop above only acts when `categoryForQuery(...)` of the preceding words is non-null.

- Line 662, `rest = rest.filter((t) => !isParking(t) && !NEGATION.has(t))`, then deletes 'degil' and 'olmasin' as filler.
- Line 694, `tokens.findIndex(isDistrictName)`, takes the first district word, which is the one the user rejected.

- "Bornova değil Buca'da kebap" gives district Bornova, placeQuery "buca", cat meat, notCat null.
- "Konak olmasın Karşıyaka'da balık" gives district Konak, placeQuery "karsiyaka".
- "Bornova'da değil Karşıyaka'da otopark" gives district Bornova, placeQuery "karsiyaka", mentionsParking true.

confirmed.description: tariffCost runs every band label through bandMinutes, which only reads the hour range and drops the vehicle class. confirmed.title: The cancel mark is never cleared, so every later call on a cancelled messageId is refunded for an hour (free AI, global counter pushed back down)
confirmed.description: cancelUse writes `cancel:${day}:${deviceId}:${messageId}` with a 1 h TTL and refunds the use. releaseIfCancelled, which runs in every respond(), checks only that this mark exists and then calls releaseUse. It never deletes or consumes the mark. After a cancel the messageId is no longer in the device list. The next call with it is charged as new (added:true) and reaches Anthropic, and respond() then finds the mark and refunds it again. This repeats on every call for an hour. Cancels also work on messages that already got their answer, so one /cancel turns a delivered message into an endless free one. Each round also takes one off the global counter.

The fingerprint matches, so there is no 409. takeUse charges M as new and Anthropic is called. respond() runs releaseIfCancelled, which sees the mark and runs releaseUse, so the response says remaining 10 and the global counter goes back down. The device keeps 10/10 uses while getting unlimited answers for 1 h, bounded only by the per-IP guard. One cancel out of MAX_CANCELS_PER_DAY is enough.
confirmed.evidence: store.ts:67-70: `case 'releaseIfCancelled': { ... if (!(await wasCancelled(kv, o.deviceId, o.messageId, now))) return null; return (await releaseUse(kv, o.deviceId, o.messageId, now)).remaining; }` has no delete of the mark. quota.ts:256-258: `await kv.put(`cancel:${day}:${deviceId}:${messageId}`, '1', { expirationTtl: CANCEL_MARK_TTL_SECONDS });` (3600). index.ts:255: `const back = await quota.releaseIfCancelled(deviceId, messageId, now);` is called on every response, including 'ok'.

The finding is real. I traced it through the code on this branch.

1. **The cancel.** cancelUse (quota.ts:242-260) raises the cancel count, writes the mark `cancel:${day}:${deviceId}:${messageId}` with a 3600 s TTL, and calls releaseUse. releaseUse takes M out of the device list (refund) and lowers `ai:global`.

2. **The next call with the same body.** In runOp 'begin' (store.ts:55-60), the stored fingerprint equals the new one, so there is no 409. takeUse (quota.ts:186) sees that M is not in the list, so `known` is false. The minIntervalMs check (1000 ms) and the global cap check pass. charge pushes M again (added:true), and takeUse writes global+1 and the `ai:last` time. index.ts then calls Anthropic.

3. **The response.** respond() always calls `quota.releaseIfCancelled` (index.ts ~255), on 'ok' as well. That op (store.ts:67-71) only checks wasCancelled. Nothing deletes or uses up the mark. It then calls releaseUse, which finds M in the list again: it removes M, lowers global by one, and the response body says remaining 10.

4. **The loop.** This repeats on every call until the mark expires (1 h, inside the same Istanbul day). One cancel out of MAX_CANCELS_PER_DAY = 5 is enough, and the cancel works on a message that already got its answer.

**Limits on the impact.** The per-IP guard (AI_DEFAULTS.perIp = 100 per day, counted on every request) still caps each IP. The per-device quota could already be dodged by sending new deviceIds, so the extra per-IP gain is limited. The new harm is to the global cap: each free call adds one to the counter and takes it off again, so on net the counter stays flat. Callers spread over many IPs can push Anthropic spend past AI_GLOBAL_DAILY, which is the spend backstop. The device quota is also bypassed: 10/10 stays shown while answers keep coming.

That fits medium, not higher.

1. **The cancel mark is never removed.** quota.ts:256 writes `cancel:${day}:${deviceId}:${messageId}` with a 3600 s TTL. The only other code that touches it is wasCancelled (quota.ts:269), which only reads it. store.ts:67-70 (releaseIfCancelled) checks the mark and calls releaseUse, and never deletes it.

2. **A replay gets past every guard.**
   - The first successful call stored callKey = fingerprint (store.ts:59). A byte-identical body gives the same fingerprint, so there is no 409 (store.ts:57).
   - cancelUse ran releaseUse, so the messageId is no longer in the `q:` list. takeUse therefore treats the next call as new: `known` is false and it calls charge, which adds it. It also adds 1 to the global counter.
   - The only checks left are minIntervalMs (1000 ms by default; it uses `ai:last`, a 60 s key) and the global cap. The client can space its calls 1 s apart.
   - Anthropic is called. Then respond() (index.ts:255) calls releaseIfCancelled for every outcome, including 'ok'. The mark is still there, so releaseUse removes the messageId again and lowers the global counter. The reply shows remaining restored.

3. **The cancel cap does not stop it.** /cancel only needs a valid-looking deviceId and messageId, and works on a message that already got its answer. One cancel, out of MAX_CANCELS_PER_DAY = 5, is enough for an hour of repeats.

So per IP, the device-quota bypass adds little; perIp (100 per day) still bounds it. The real harm is to the global cap (AI_GLOBAL_DAILY = 10000), which limits spend. Each repeat adds 1 to the counter and then takes it off again, so the counter does not grow. Callers from many IPs could then send Anthropic calls well beyond the global daily cap, which normally stops spend at 10000 calls a day.

A real client can hit this by accident too: after a timeout cancel, any later stage call with the same messageId is free. Because perIp still applies, I rate it medium, not high.

I confirmed the mechanism from the code. cancelUse (quota.ts:242-260) writes `cancel:${day}:${deviceId}:${messageId}` with a 3600 s TTL and removes M from the device list through releaseUse. The 'releaseIfCancelled' op (store.ts:67-70) only checks that the mark exists (wasCancelled, quota.ts:263-269) and then calls releaseUse. Nothing ever deletes or uses up the mark.

Here is the replay. After the cancel, the same /understand body is sent again:
1. begin (store.ts:55-60) finds previous === fingerprint, so there is no 409.
2. takeUse (quota.ts:186) sees known=false. The only checks are the 1 s interval and the global cap. charge adds M back (added:true) and raises ai:global.
3. Anthropic is called.
4. respond() (index.ts:255) calls releaseIfCancelled on every outcome, including 'ok'. It finds the mark, and releaseUse takes M back off and lowers ai:global again.

This repeats for an hour. Nothing in the comments, tests or history says it is intended. The cancelUse docstring describes the mark as being for "a handler that is still running (or one that has not charged yet)". worker.test.ts only covers a repeated /cancel and a cancel while the call is in flight, never a new call after a cancel. The only commit that touches this code (da58d22) is about races.

Mitigating factors:
- deviceId is any client-supplied string that passes ID_RE, with no authentication. So the per-device 10/day quota and MAX_CANCELS_PER_DAY (also per device) can already be dodged by rotating deviceIds. On that side the bug adds little.
- The per-IP guard (100/day across all endpoints) still applies.
- The real client (src/lib/ai/client.ts:214) only cancels after a timeout and does not reuse the messageId, so normal users are not affected.

What this bug adds is beyond deviceId rotation: calls on a cancelled messageId always lower ai:global back to where it was. That cap is the daily spending ceiling on Anthropic (AI_GLOBAL_DAILY, 10000 by default). Calls made with rotated deviceIds still count toward it; calls made this way never do. An attacker with many IPs (one cancel each, using a fresh deviceId) can therefore spend Anthropic money past the global cap, held back only by the 100/day per-IP limit and the 1 s interval.

This is a real cost-control and quota defect, not a nit. It needs several IPs to do much damage and the per-IP limit still holds, so I rate it medium rather than high.

confirmed.title: Cached live isOpen flag is trusted indefinitely: an offline or cached result keeps showing car parks as closed or open from an old snapshot
confirmed.description: İSPARK (isparkProvider.ts:106) and İzmir (izmirProvider.ts:103) store the source's momentary open/closed flag in Parking.isOpen. deviceCache saves it with the result. primeParkingsFromCache and the offline fallback in loadParkings (repository.ts:111) bring it back with no expiry. openState returns that flag before looking at opening hours or the clock: freshness.ts hides stale free counts after 15 minutes, but nothing ages isOpen. The reverse also happens: a park cached while open at 22:00 is shown open, with no 'maybe closed' hint, at 02:00.

confirmed.title: Per-IP AI limit is keyed on the full IPv6 address, so one host can rotate addresses within its /64 and use up the global daily AI cap for everyone
confirmed.description: The Worker's only protection against abuse that does not depend on the client is the per-IP counter (the deviceId is chosen by the client and any value passes isId). ipGuard keys that counter on the raw CF-Connecting-IP string. On IPv6, a single subscriber or VPS normally owns a whole /64, which is 2^64 addresses. Each address gets its own 100 calls a day, and each request can carry a fresh random deviceId, so neither the per-device quota nor the 1 s interval applies. Only AI_GLOBAL_DAILY (10000) is left, and it is shared by all users. Once it is used up, takeUse returns reason 'global' for every real user until midnight Istanbul time. The operator also pays for about 10k Haiku calls.

They change the source address inside their /64 every 100 requests (about 100 addresses in total) and pick a new deviceId each time. After about 10000 requests, ai:global:<day> reaches the cap. From then until the day changes, every real user's chat message gets a 429 {reason:'global'} and the assistant falls back to rules only.

confirmed.title: Results header claims '0 free' when no car park has a known count; the 'unknown' summary can never show

confirmed.description: verifyPlan rejects a closed car park (`if (!park || park.openState === 'closed') return null;`), but verifyParkPick has no such check. It only needs one reason that holds. askParkPick does not filter closed parks either: runPark builds the cards from every car park in the radius, with no open filter. For a trip (meta.planWhen !== null, minCards = 1), finishAnswer turns the verified pick straight into parkOnlyPlan ('leave the car here, walk to X').

The nearest car park closes at 19:00, so its candidate has openState 'closed', which parkOpenAt computes from the hours at the planned time. The model returns pick = that park with reasons ['closest'] or ['free']. parkReasonHolds('closest') is true, so verifyParkPick returns it. The app shows a plan whose first step is to park at a car park that is closed when the user arrives. A 'now' park pick of a park that is closed now is accepted the same way.

confirmed.title: A failed AsyncStorage read or write during hydration leaves the app stuck on the splash screen for good
confirmed.description: RootLayout only renders once `useHydrated()` is true (`const ready = (fontsLoaded || !!fontError) && hydrated; ... if (!ready) return null;`), and the splash screen only hides when `ready` is true. `useHydrated` reads `useApp.persist.hasHydrated()`, which zustand 5.0.15 sets to true only on the success path of `hydrate()` (node_modules/zustand/middleware.js:430-434). Any error in that chain goes to `.catch` (line 435), which only calls `postRehydrationCallback`. The app store in src/store/app.ts:141-181 sets no `onRehydrateStorage`, and nothing else ever sets hydrated or hides the splash. Three things can reject the chain: (1) `JSON.parse` inside `createJSONStorage().getItem` throws on a truncated or corrupt `yerim-var/app` value; (2) `AsyncStorage.getItem` itself rejects; (3) after a migration (`migrated === true` for any stored version 1 or 2), zustand awaits `setItem()` before setting hasHydrated, so a write failure (e.g. a full disk) also lands in `.catch`, even though the merged state was already applied. The sanitizers in migrate.ts only guard against bad values inside parsed JSON, never against parse or storage errors.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The app is killed partway through a write, or the device storage is full, so the AsyncStorage value for 'yerim-var/app' is the truncated string '{"state":{"onboarded":tru'. On the next launch, JSON.parse throws, the hydrate promise rejects, hasHydrated stays false, RootLayout returns null, and SplashScreen.hideAsync is never called. The user sees the splash forever. No state change can happen to overwrite the bad value, so this repeats on every launch until the user clears app data or reinstalls. The same happens to a v1/v2 user upgrading to v3 on a full disk: the migrate write rejects and the app never leaves the splash.

src/store/useHydrated.ts:6: `const get = () => useApp.persist.hasHydrated();`
node_modules/zustand/middleware.js:424-440: `set(stateFromStorage, true); if (migrated) { return setItem(); } }).then(() => { ... hasHydrated = true; finishHydrationListeners.forEach(...) }).catch((e) => { ... postRehydrationCallback == null ? void 0 : postRehydrationCallback(void 0, e); });`

confirmed.title: Router is told to call itself "Yerim Var asistanı", but validateFreeText drops every chat reply that does
confirmed.description: understandSystem (protocol.ts:420) says: "Kendinden söz edersen yalnızca \"Yerim Var asistanı\" de". The chat reply is then shown only if validateFreeText('chat', ...) passes (assistant.ts:863). In the capitalisation check, a capitalised word that is not at the start of a sentence must be in KNOWN_CAPITALISED. That list has 'Yerim' (the comment points to the old "Ben Yerim" wording) but not 'Var'. So "Var" after "Yerim" is always a capitalised word in the middle of a sentence, and the reply is rejected. The test at freeText.test.ts:167 still checks the old 'Ben Yerim' wording, so the clash is never tested.
confirmed.failure_scenario: User asks "sen kimsin?" or "bu uygulama ne yapıyor?". The router does what its prompt says and answers "Merhaba, ben Yerim Var asistanı! In validateFreeText, 'Var' has startsUpper=true and atStart=false, and fold('Var')='var' is not in KNOWN_CAPITALISED, so it returns null. chatFromRouter returns null and the app shows its fixed template every time. confirmed.title: İSPARK tariff refresh can overwrite the file after losing up to half of the car parks' official prices
confirmed.description: The header says 'A failed or thin run keeps the previous file', but the only guard compares this run's tariff count with this run's own Park list (MIN_SHARE = 0.5). Nothing compares it with the previous file. Each ParkDetay call gets 2 attempts with a 20 s timeout, and any failure is dropped silently. So a run where the İBB API rate-limits or times out part of the requests still writes the file if at least 50% succeed. The same happens if /Park returns a short list (for example 10 parks, all with tariffs): it passes the guard and replaces the full file. fetch-sources.mjs uses a 70%-of-previous guard (writeData), but this script has none.
confirmed.failure_scenario: data/tariffs-ispark.json now has 244 tariffs. In the weekly run (or a push to claude/**), ParkDetay times out for 120 parks and 124 succeed. 124 >= 244*0.5, so the file is rewritten with 124 tariffs. On a push event it is committed straight to the branch; on schedule it becomes a PR. 120 İstanbul car parks lose their 'official' prices in the app (src/data/tariffs.ts imports this file).
confirmed.evidence: scripts/fetch-ispark-tariffs.mjs:64-79 `for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 2; attempt++) { ... setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 20_000) ... } return null;`; :100 `if (row) tariffs.push(row);`; :105 `if (tariffs.length < ids.length * MIN_SHARE) {` (MIN_SHARE = 0.5, line 15). confirmed.title: Location picker sends the exact unrounded GPS fix to Apple reverse geocoding, which the privacy texts do not disclose
confirmed.description: With no lat/lng param, konum-sec gets the user's current location and calls lookup(loc), which calls reverseStreet(loc). That runs Location.reverseGeocodeAsync with the full-precision coordinates (src/lib/location.ts:69), and on iOS this goes to Apple's geocoding service. The app rounds to about 100 m (roundArea) only for the Apple car-park search. The in-app privacy text (tr.ts:329: 'yazdığın metin ve yaklaşık bölgen (~100 m) Apple Haritalar'a gider') and the Apple Maps row of docs/gizlilik.html list only typed text, the rounded ~100 m search area and map imagery. Neither mentions that the precise GPS position is sent to Apple.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A user who has granted location opens 'Ev/İş kaydet' or 'Haritadan seç' (konum-sec without coordinates). currentLocation(false, 3000) returns e.g. 38.462817,27.216734. After the debounce, reverseGeocodeAsync({latitude: 38.462817, longitude: 27.216734}) sends that exact point to Apple. The privacy notice says only a ~100 m approximate area is sent.

**What the code does.** In src/app/konum-sec.tsx:70-79, when no lat/lng param is given, the screen calls `currentLocation(false, 3000)`. It then calls `lookup(loc)`, which runs after a debounce (lines 58-66) and calls `reverseStreet(p)`.   - the ~100 m rounded area for car-park search;

- MapKit tiles for the zoomed-in view, and the IP address, already reveal roughly where the user is.
- No secret leaks to an untrusted third party.

confirmed.title: Production EAS profile reuses iOS build number 1, so the second App Store upload is rejected
confirmed.description: eas.json sets "appVersionSource": "local", so EAS reads the iOS build number from app.json. app.json hard-codes "buildNumber": "1", and the production profile is empty: it has no "autoIncrement": true. Every production build therefore ships CFBundleVersion 1.

Bumping buildNumber by hand before each build is also a normal workflow with local versioning. The finding's line "release is blocked until someone edits app.json by hand" describes that ordinary manual step, not an outage.

confirmed.title: A message that spans Istanbul midnight is charged twice, and its /cancel refund is lost, because each call re-derives the day
confirmed.description: takeUse treats a messageId as 'known' (already charged, so free) only if it appears in today's list `q:${day}:${deviceId}`, where day comes from that request's own `now`. The /understand and the /pick or /plan of one user message are separate requests. When they fall on either side of 00:00 Istanbul, the follow-up is not 'known'. It then goes through the min-interval check against `ai:last:${deviceId}`, which is not day-scoped, so it gets 429 'slow' if it arrives within 1 s. Otherwise it is charged as a second new use on the new day and counted again in the global counter. /cancel has the same problem: cancelUse writes the mark under the new day, and releaseUse looks for the messageId in the new day's list. The still-running /understand handler checks `cancel:${oldDay}:...` with its own start time. So the use charged on the old day is never given back, although the client timed out and asked for the refund.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A user sends a message at 23:59:58 Istanbul time. /understand charges M on day D (9 left). At 00:00:01 the app calls /pick with the same M. On day D+1, M is not in the list, and now - last < 1000 ms, so the server returns 429 'slow' and the pick falls back to rules. If the pick arrives after 1 s, it is charged as a new message on D+1 (9 left on the new day for a single message). Another case: /understand starts at 23:59:55 and the client times out at 00:00:07 and calls /cancel. The refund looks in the D+1 list and finds nothing. The handler's releaseIfCancelled checks the D mark and finds nothing. The day-D use stays charged.

confirmed.title: A Bursa municipal point with no name and only a capacity deletes every OSM car park within 80 m, including named and differently tagged ones
confirmed.description: The header comment (lines 10-12) says Açık Yeşil data is 'merged (capacity only)'. In fact fromBursaRow builds full replacement records with name possibly null and isPaid/isIndoor/nonstop/openingHoursText/address all null. A row is kept with no name as long as it has a capacity (`if (!rawName && !capacity) return null;`). Those records then go into `official`, and every OSM car park within 80 m of any official record is dropped, with no check on name or type. Nothing is merged into the OSM record: its name, fee, indoor flag, hours, operator, address, accessibility tags and `near` label are lost. A neighbouring but different car park inside the 80 m radius is deleted too. The municipal record also never gets a `near` name, so the user sees an unnamed car park.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The Açık Yeşil portal comes back (it is unreachable in the current report) and publishes a GeoJSON point with only a 'kapasite' column at a city-centre multi-storey garage. OSM has 'X Katlı Otopark' with fee=yes, building=parking and opening_hours, plus a separate surface car park 60 m away. After the refresh, both OSM records are removed from data/parkings-static-bursa.json. They are replaced by a single record with name null, isPaid null, isIndoor null and no hours, so the app loses the name, price flag, indoor filter and hours for those car parks. The 70% shrink guard does not catch it, because only a few records change.

confirmed.title: Privacy manifest says the app collects no data, but it sends a device ID and chat text off the device
confirmed.description: ios.privacyManifests sets NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes to an empty array. That tells Apple no data leaves the device and is kept. The app does send data that is kept. A random deviceId is stored in src/store/ai.ts:37 and sent on every AI and quota call. The worker keeps it in its quota store under keys like `ai:call:${day}:${deviceId}:${messageId}:${path}` (server/yerim-ai/src/index.ts:205). The in-app privacy text says this ID is kept for up to 2 days. The chat text the user types is also sent to Anthropic's Claude through the worker. Apple counts data as 'collected' when it is sent off the device and kept longer than it takes to answer the request in real time. So the app collects a Device ID (used for App Functionality) and Other User Content, and the manifest should list both.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The app is submitted with a manifest that declares no collected data. That does not match what the app sends: every /understand, /pick or /quota request carries the deviceId, and the server keeps it for the daily counter. Apple can flag the manifest as inaccurate or reject the app at review. Users also see a 'no data collected' declaration that is wrong.

confirmed.title: External deep link yerimvar://sohbet?q=... sends attacker-chosen text to the AI (and spends quota) with no user action
confirmed.description: The chat screen sends the `q` route param as a user message as soon as it mounts. Expo Router maps the app's custom scheme (app.json `"scheme": "yerimvar"`) straight onto routes, and there is no `+native-intent` file or other check on where a link came from. So any web page, QR code, push link or other app can open `yerimvar://sohbet?q=<text>`, and the app sends that text right away. For a user who has given Yerim AI consent (`aiOn`), the message goes through `deps.ai.understand` to the Cloudflare worker and on to Anthropic, and it uses up one of their 10 daily AI messages. If the text asks for something nearby (e.g. 'yakınımda kebap'), `deps.here` reads the device GPS and /pick runs with candidates around the user's real position, all without the user typing or confirming anything. The consent only covers 'messages you write' (gizlilik: 'Yazdığın mesaj'), not text injected by a third party.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A user has accepted Yerim AI. A web page runs `location.href='yerimvar://sohbet?q=yak%C4%B1n%C4%B1mda%20kebap'`, or the link is opened 10 times in a row. Each time the app opens the chat and the mount effect calls `send(q)`. This reads the location, calls /understand and then /pick on the worker, and Anthropic receives text and nearby candidates the user never wrote. Repeated opens use up the whole daily quota (10/day), and once the quota is gone the user's own AI questions fall back to the rule-based answers.

There is no src/app/+native-intent.tsx to filter incoming links (ls src/app). The only intended callers are internal (src/components/home/SearchCard.tsx:17, src/app/ara.tsx:43).

confirmed.title: Restaurant detail says 'no car park nearby' during the first download instead of 'loading'
confirmed.description: The car-park section picks its empty-state text from `isLoading`. `useParkings()` always sets `placeholderData: STATIC_ONLY_PLACEHOLDER` (src/data/useParkings.ts:82), and in TanStack Query v5 (^5.104.1) a query showing placeholder data has status 'success'. While the first live download is still running, `ranked` only holds the bundled static car parks. If none of those is within 1 km, the user is told definitively that there is no parking nearby. Other screens handle this case: otopark/[id].tsx:66 and sonuc.tsx:447 also check `isPlaceholderData`.

confirmed.title: Home 'en yakın N dk' line shows the walk to a promoted live car park, not the nearest one

confirmed.title: Unnamed car park names are translated once and cached, so switching language leaves them in the old language

confirmed.title: Dish-note filter drops normal encyclopedic Turkish ('önemli bir yeri', 'unlu', 've/veya')
confirmed.description: For dishNote, DISH_NOTE_PLACE_TOKENS `/^yer(i|ler|leri|de|lerde|e|in)?$/` treats every standalone 'yeri' as a reference to a place, but 'X mutfağında önemli bir yeri vardır/olan' ('has an important place in X cuisine') is a stock phrase in dish descriptions. The BANNED_WORDS entry 'unlu' (meant for 'ünlü', famous) folds to the same text as 'unlu' (made with flour), which is the normal word for pastry and bread dishes ('unlu mamul', 'unlu bir kahvaltılık'). URL_LIKE's `\b[a-z0-9-]+\/[a-z0-9]` also rejects plain 've/veya'. The prompt allows none of these to be banned, so the model has no reason to avoid them, and the note about an unfamiliar dish (the point of Z3) is silently lost.

The router writes dishNote 'Boyoz, Ege mutfağında önemli bir yeri olan yağlı bir hamur işidir.' or 'Pişi, mayalı hamurdan kızartılarak yapılan unlu bir kahvaltılıktır.' validateFreeText returns null for both (checked with bun), so the user gets no dish explanation.

confirmed.title: Calls the user can force to fail are refunded even though Anthropic billed them, so neither the device limit nor the global cap counts them
confirmed.description: Every non-ok outcome calls giveBack(), which removes the messageId from the device list and lowers ai:global. That includes outcomes where Anthropic did produce (and bill) output: structured output cut off at max_tokens or not matching the schema (readable() returns null, or parsed_output is missing), a refusal, or an empty /chat reply. The request text is user-controlled, so a client can make these outcomes happen on purpose, for example by asking for a very long value so /understand's JSON is cut at 2048 output tokens, or the /chat JSON at 200 tokens. After the refund the messageId is new again, so the same request can be repeated. These calls never count against the 10/day device limit or the global cap.

The SDK cannot parse the truncated JSON, readable() returns null, unknown() runs giveBack(), and the response is 200 {understanding:{kind:'unknown'}, remaining:10}. The client sends it again every ~1 s (only the interval applies). Each call is a full-length billed Anthropic completion, yet /quota still reports 10 remaining and ai:global stays near 0, so the global cost ceiling never trips. Only the per-IP 100/day guard limits it.

confirmed.title: Search 'P' suggestion can show a nearby different car park's free count when its own count is stale
confirmed.description: freeForHit loops over every car park within 60 m of the hit, but it only narrows `bestD` when it finds a car park whose count may be shown. If the car park at the hit's own spot (for example 3 m away) has a stale count, `visibleFree` gives null for it and it is skipped. A different car park up to 60 m away that has a fresh count then wins. TypingState shows that number as a green 'N boş' badge, and in the a11y label, on the row named after the searched car park. The rule was meant to skip a static OSM/İzelman duplicate of the same car park (that is what the test covers), but it also skips the hit's own live record when that record is merely stale.

confirmed.title: Chat messages typed before AI consent are sent to Anthropic as history once the user taps 'Aç'
confirmed.description: The composer stays enabled while consent is still 'unknown', since the ConsentCard is only a list header. Messages typed in that state are answered by the local rules, but they still go into `messages`. `bindAi` runs for every message whether AI is on or not, and copies the last HISTORY_LIMIT (10) messages into `aiMsgRef.current.history`. When the user then taps 'Aç' and sends one more message, `understand` sends `...bound`, history included, and client.ts:208 passes the history through `clipHistory(req.history, HISTORY_LIMIT, ...)`. So up to ten turns written before consent, user text included, go to the Cloudflare worker and on to Anthropic. The consent text and the privacy policy describe consent as forward-looking: 'Açarsan sohbete yazdığın mesajlar ... gönderilir' and 'Onay vermezsen uygulama kendi kurallarıyla cevap verir'. Under KVKK, explicit consent has to come before processing.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A fresh install opens Sohbet, where the consent card shows. The user ignores the card and types 'Evim Kıbrıs Şehitleri 45, yakında otopark?'. The rules engine answers locally and nothing is sent. The user then taps 'Aç' and types 'köfte'. The /understand request body now carries history [{role:'user', text:'Evim Kıbrıs Şehitleri 45, yakında otopark?'}, {role:'bot', ...}], and that text reaches Anthropic even though it was written before consent.

Line 371: `{aiClient && consent === 'unknown' ? <ConsentCard onChoose={setConsent} /> : null}` sits in the list header, and the Composer is not disabled. Lines 135-142: `understand: async (...) => { const bound = aiMsgRef.current; const req = { ...bound, deviceId: ... }`. src/lib/ai/client.ts:208: `history: clipHistory(req.history, HISTORY_LIMIT, MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS)`. Nothing filters out turns written before consent.

Nothing marks a message as written before consent, so the rules-engine turns from the 'unknown' state stay in `messages`.

The ConsentCard (line 371) sits only in the ListHeaderComponent. The Composer (line 390) is never disabled, so the user can type before choosing. confirmed.title: Static/live merge drops distinct car parks: any static record within 80 m of any live record is treated as a duplicate
confirmed.description: withStatic() treats nearness as identity: a bundled (İzelman/OSM) car park is removed whenever any live record lies within DUPLICATE_RADIUS_M = 80 m. It never checks the name, type or capacity. Live İzmir and İSPARK feeds include many short on-street segments ('Yol Kenarı', 'YOL ÜSTÜ') in dense centres. Each one hides every other car park within 80 m: a different street's segment, or a street segment next to a multi-storey car park. The one-to-one match (the static twin of the live record) is correct, but the extra matches lose real car parks from the list and the map.

Yol Kenarı Otopark' correctly matches 'Plevne Bulvarı - 1 Yol Kenarı Otoparkı' at 29 m, but it also removes the separate 'Mustafa Bey Cd. -2 Yol Kenarı Otoparkı' (52 bays) at 69 m. Live 'Konak Katlı Otopark' correctly matches 'Konak Katlı Otoparkı' at 37 m, but it also removes 'Konak Doğum Hastanesi (Karşısı) Yol Kenarı Otoparkı' (25 bays) at 79 m. Used for every non-mock result in src/data/useParkings.ts:70 `out = { ...result, parkings: withStatic(result.parkings) };`. Distances computed from src/data/__tests__/fixtures/izmir-live-2026-10-07.json against data/parkings-static.json: Plevne->Mustafa Bey Cd.-2 69 m, Konak Katlı->Konak Doğum Hastanesi Yol Kenarı 79 m.

A live car park within 80 m is still shown, so the user is never left without parking nearby. What they lose are alternative car parks and their capacity, which reappear only when live data is empty. confirmed.title: Park pick 'open_now' is checked against the planned time but shown as 'su an acik' (open now)
confirmed.description: parkReasonHolds('open_now') returns `c.openState === 'open'`. confirmed.title: 'closest' is checked on rounded walk minutes, so a farther candidate passes as 'the closest'
confirmed.description: pickReasonHolds, planReasonHolds and parkReasonHolds all check 'closest' as `c.walkMin === Math.min(...all.map((x) => x.walkMin))`. walkMin comes from walkMinFromMeters, which is `Math.max(1, Math.round(m*1.3/80))`: every distance up to about 92 m is 1 min, and about 92-153 m is 2 min. The candidates carry only rounded minutes, so the verifier cannot tell which place is really nearest. Any candidate in the same minute bucket as the nearest one passes. The unit test treats this as intended ('ties count'), but the text shown is the absolute claim 'en yakin olani' / 'it's the closest'.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Candidates: A at 30 m and D at 90 m, both walkMin 1. The model picks D with reasons ['closest']. The check passes, and the user reads 'D: en yakin olani (~1 dk yurume)', with D shown first, although A is three times closer and is also in the list.
confirmed.evidence: verify.ts:47-48 `case 'closest': return c.walkMin === Math.min(...all.map((x) => x.walkMin));`. verify.ts:26-28 `return Math.max(1, Math.round((m * 1.3) / 80));`. assistant.ts:2289 `walkMin: walkMinFromMeters(card.distanceM)`. tr.ts:714 `closest: 'en yakin olani (~{{count}} dk yurume)'`. verify.test.ts:87 `'"closest" needs the smallest walk; ties count'`.
